title: 5 taste terms every wine drinker should know
subtitle: These are the words sommeliers use. Here's what they actually mean for your glass.

sections.plain: How heavy a wine feels in your mouth
sections.detail: Think of it like milk: skimmed versus whole. A light-bodied wine feels delicate and clean; a full-bodied wine feels rich and coat-your-mouth weighty. Alcohol is the main driver — wines above 13.5% ABV typically feel fuller.
examples: Light: Pinot Grigio, Pinot Noir, Vinho Verde
Medium: Merlot, Grenache, Viognier
Full: Cabernet Sauvignon, Barolo, oaked Chardonnay

sections.plain: That drying grip on your gums after you swallow
sections.detail: Tannins come from grape skins, seeds, stems, and oak barrels. They create that dry, slightly astringent sensation — like biting into an unripe banana or drinking strong black tea. High-tannin wines age brilliantly; low-tannin wines are approachable young.
examples: High: Barolo, Nebbiolo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat
Medium: Merlot, Syrah, Sangiovese, Malbec
Low: Pinot Noir, Grenache, Gamay, Barbera

sections.plain: How zingy and fresh the wine tastes
sections.detail: Acidity is what makes your mouth water. High-acid wines feel bright, crisp, and food-friendly — they cut through fat and cleanse the palate. Low-acid wines feel softer, rounder, and more plush. If you love Sauvignon Blanc, you love high acidity.
examples: High: Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Chablis, Pinot Grigio
Medium: Chardonnay (oaked), Grenache, Sangiovese
Low: Viognier, Gewürztraminer, Muscat Blanc

sections.plain: From bone dry to lusciously sweet
sections.detail: Most table wines are dry — yeast converts nearly all grape sugar into alcohol during fermentation. Off-dry wines have a subtle sweetness. Dessert wines are intentionally sweet, either from late harvest, noble rot, or stopping fermentation early.
examples: Bone dry: Muscadet, Chablis, most Champagne (Brut)
Off-dry: Spätlese Riesling, Vouvray demi-sec, Gewürztraminer
Sweet: Sauternes, Tokaji, Port, Moscato d'Asti

sections.plain: How long the flavour lingers after you swallow
sections.detail: The finish is the aftertaste — how long the wine's flavours persist after swallowing. A great wine has a long, evolving finish. Sommeliers measure this in caudalies: each cauda equals one second of lingering flavour. 10 seconds is good; 30+ is exceptional.
examples: Short: Most entry-level wines (under £12)
Medium: Mid-range bottles — a pleasant 5–10 seconds
Long: Premier Cru Burgundy, Barolo Riserva, Grand Cru Alsace

title: How wine actually gets made
subtitle: Same starting point — grapes — and three decisions that split it into red, white, and everything between.

sections.plain: Yeast eats sugar, sugar becomes alcohol
sections.detail: Wild or added yeast consumes the natural sugar in grape juice and converts it into alcohol and carbon dioxide. Left alone, this takes days to weeks. Stop it early and sugar remains — that's how off-dry and sweet wines are made on purpose.
examples: Dry wine: fermentation runs to completion
Off-dry: fermentation stopped partway
Sparkling: a second fermentation traps the CO2 in the bottle or tank

sections.plain: The single decision that makes a wine red, white, rosé, or orange
sections.detail: Grape juice itself is pale — colour and tannin come from leaving crushed skins in contact with the juice during fermentation. Reds ferment with skins in for weeks; rosé gets a few hours; white wine is pressed off the skins almost immediately; orange wine is white grapes given the red-wine treatment.
examples: Red: days to weeks on skins
Rosé: hours on skins, then pressed off
Orange: white grapes fermented on skins like a red

sections.plain: What the wine sits in before bottling changes how it tastes
sections.detail: Stainless steel keeps fruit flavours sharp and unchanged. Oak barrels let in tiny amounts of oxygen and contribute vanilla, toast, or spice depending on the barrel. Concrete and clay sit between the two — neutral, but breathable.
examples: Steel: crisp Sauvignon Blanc, most rosé
Oak: Rioja, Barolo, buttery Chardonnay
Concrete/clay: many natural and orange wines

title: Reading a label without guessing
subtitle: Four lines of text tell you almost everything — once you know where to look.

sections.plain: The name usually matters more than the grape
sections.detail: European labels often lead with the estate or village rather than the grape variety, because the region implies the grape by law. A Chablis is legally Chardonnay; a Barolo is legally Nebbiolo. New World labels tend to name the grape directly instead.
examples: Old World: region name = Chablis, Barolo, Rioja
New World: grape name = Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon
Both can appear together on the same label

sections.plain: The year and the place set your expectations
sections.detail: The vintage is simply the year the grapes were picked, and the region narrows down climate and style before you've tasted a drop. A cool-region Chardonnay and a warm-region Chardonnay from the same year can taste like different grapes entirely.
examples: Cool region: higher acid, lighter body
Warm region: riper fruit, fuller body
"NV" means non-vintage — a deliberate house-style blend

sections.plain: The ABV percentage is a shortcut to body and dryness
sections.detail: Higher alcohol usually means riper grapes and fuller body; lower alcohol often signals a lighter, sometimes off-dry style. German Riesling labels also carry Prädikat terms (Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese) that rank from lightest/driest to sweetest.
examples: Under 11.5%: often lighter or off-dry
11.5–13.5%: typical dry table wine range
Over 14%: full-bodied, ripe, often New World

title: Old World vs New World, in practice
subtitle: A geography split, not a quality one — but it does predict what's in the glass.

sections.plain: Where the wine is from, not how good it is
sections.detail: Old World means Europe and the Mediterranean, where winemaking traditions and regional laws go back centuries. New World means everywhere those traditions were exported to more recently — the Americas, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa.
examples: Old World: France, Italy, Spain, Germany, Greece
New World: USA, Argentina, Chile, Australia, South Africa
Neither is a marker of quality — both make wine at every price point

sections.plain: Restraint versus ripeness, as a general tendency
sections.detail: Old World regions are often cooler and more regulated, tending toward earthier, higher-acid, lower-alcohol wines. New World regions are often sunnier with fewer legal restrictions, tending toward riper fruit, fuller body, and more obvious oak.
examples: Old World tendency: earth, mineral, restraint
New World tendency: ripe fruit, richness, boldness
Cool-climate New World regions blur this constantly

sections.plain: Climate explains more than the continent does
sections.detail: A cool-climate Australian Chardonnay from the Yarra Valley can taste closer to Burgundy than to a warm-climate Californian one. Treat Old World/New World as a starting guess about style, then let climate and producer choices correct it.
examples: Yarra Valley (Australia) Chardonnay: cool, restrained
Central Valley (California) Chardonnay: warm, ripe
Both are "New World" — climate decided the style, not the map

title: Serving temperature and glassware actually matter
subtitle: The same bottle can taste flabby or shut down depending on how it's poured.

sections.plain: Temperature changes what you can actually taste
sections.detail: Serve red wine too warm and alcohol dominates, making it taste hot and flat. Serve white or sparkling wine too cold and it mutes aroma and flavour almost entirely. Most reds are served noticeably too warm at room temperature in a heated house.
examples: Light reds & rosé: 12–14°C, lightly chilled
Full-bodied reds: 16–18°C, cooler than "room temperature"
Whites & sparkling: 7–10°C, but not fridge-cold for long

sections.plain: Not snobbery — the bowl shape genuinely changes aroma
sections.detail: A wider bowl exposes more surface area to air, releasing more aroma; a narrower opening concentrates that aroma toward your nose. That's why a big Burgundy glass and a narrow flute exist for different reasons, not for show.
examples: Wide bowl: reds, aromatic whites
Narrow tulip: delicate whites and most everyday use
Flute: preserves bubbles in sparkling wine longer

sections.plain: Pouring into a separate vessel does two different jobs
sections.detail: For a young, tannic red, decanting adds oxygen and softens the wine within 30–60 minutes. For an old red with sediment, decanting slowly separates the clear wine from the grit at the bottom of the bottle — a different job, done more gently.
examples: Young tannic red: pour vigorously, let it breathe
Old red with sediment: pour slowly and stop before the sediment
Most whites and light reds: don't need it at all

title: What vintage really tells you
subtitle: It's a weather report stamped on the bottle, not a scorecard.

sections.plain: The year records the growing season, not the wine's rank
sections.detail: Vintage reflects the specific year's rainfall, sunshine, and temperature during the growing season — it isn't a fixed grade a region earns every year. A cool, wet year in one region can be a great year in a warmer one nearby.
examples: Warm, dry year: riper, fuller-bodied wines
Cool, wet year: lighter, higher-acid wines
Vintage variation matters more in marginal, cooler climates

sections.plain: Non-vintage is a deliberate choice, not a lesser one
sections.detail: Producers of NV Champagne and many sparkling wines blend multiple years on purpose, to keep a consistent house style year after year regardless of that year's weather. It's a different goal from vintage wine, not a downgrade.
examples: NV Champagne: consistency across years
Vintage Champagne: only made in exceptional years
Port: NV blends are everyday; vintage Port is declared rarely

sections.plain: The colder or more marginal the climate, the more the year matters
sections.detail: In warm, reliable climates like much of California or Australia, vintage-to-vintage differences are often small. In cooler, marginal regions like Burgundy, Champagne, or Germany, one bad year can mean a genuinely different wine.
examples: Marginal climates: Burgundy, Champagne, Mosel — vintage matters a lot
Reliable climates: much of California, Australia — vintage matters less
When in doubt, ask what the year was actually like locally

title: Keeping a bottle once it's open
subtitle: Oxygen is the thing working against you, and it's slower than you think.

sections.plain: Oxygen, not time, is what changes an open wine
sections.detail: Once a cork is pulled, oxygen starts reacting with the wine — the same process that eventually turns wine to vinegar, just much slower at first. Light and heat speed the process up; a cool, dark spot slows it down.
examples: Oxidation dulls fruit and turns wine flat and brownish
Heat and light accelerate the process
A capped, cool fridge is the simplest defence

sections.plain: Longer than the myths suggest, for most bottles
sections.detail: A resealed bottle in the fridge holds up far better than people assume. Light-bodied whites and sparkling fade fastest; full-bodied reds and fortified wines like Port or Sherry can last for days or even weeks.
examples: Sparkling wine: 1–3 days with a proper stopper
Light whites & rosé: 3–5 days, refrigerated
Full reds, Port, Sherry: up to a week or more

sections.plain: Two habits do most of the work
sections.detail: Push the cork back in (or use any bottle stopper) and put the bottle in the fridge — even a red, briefly, just to slow the chemistry — then let it warm up again before pouring. Smaller headspace also helps: a half-empty bottle oxidises faster than a nearly-full one.
examples: Reseal and refrigerate, even for reds
Let a chilled red warm up 20–30 minutes before pouring
Pour into a smaller bottle if you're down to the last glass

title: When a wine's gone wrong
subtitle: A handful of specific, recognisable faults — not just "I don't like this."

sections.plain: A musty, wet-cardboard smell that flattens the fruit
sections.detail: Caused by a compound called TCA contaminating the cork, corked wine smells like a damp basement or wet newspaper and mutes the fruit underneath. It has nothing to do with actual cork fragments floating in the glass.
examples: Smell: wet cardboard, musty basement, damp newspaper
Affects roughly 1–3% of cork-sealed bottles
Screwcap and synthetic-cork wines can't get this fault

sections.plain: Flat, brownish, and tastes like it's already past its best
sections.detail: Too much oxygen exposure — from a faulty seal, poor storage, or just too much time — turns fresh fruit flavours dull and nutty, and can shift the colour toward brown or amber before its time.
examples: White wine turning notably golden or brown early
Flat, sherry-like aromas in a wine that isn't meant to be Sherry
Often paired with a flat, lifeless finish

sections.plain: A short list worth recognising by smell
sections.detail: Volatile acidity smells like nail-polish remover or vinegar. Reduction smells like struck matches or rotten eggs (though this sometimes blows off with swirling). Brett smells like a barnyard or Band-Aid. All are winemaking issues, not your palate being wrong.
examples: Volatile acidity: nail polish, vinegar
Reduction: struck match, rotten egg — try swirling first
Brett: barnyard, leather, Band-Aid

sections.plain: A genuinely faulty bottle is a returnable one
sections.detail: At a restaurant, a corked or clearly faulty bottle is meant to be sent back — that's exactly what the ritual of tasting before pouring is for. At a shop, most retailers will refund or replace a faulty bottle if you bring it back.
examples: Restaurant: flag it before the table is poured, not after
Shop: keep the receipt and the bottle, most will replace it
Simply disliking the style isn't a fault — faults are specific and identifiable
